extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in coding theory and computational algebra; users of the SINGULAR software and its decodegb library
extracted.subtask_description: Formulating and solving decoding problems for linear/cyclic/affine codes using Gröbner-basis methods and related algebraic systems (CRHT, Newton identities, Fitzgerald–Lax, quadratic-equation approaches). Includes procedures to compute syndromes, construct syndrome ideals, produce general error-locator polynomials, and recover error locations/values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding problem (complete decoding; bounded up to half the minimum distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete decoding: Given y ∈ F_q^n and a code C ⊆ F_q^n, so that y is at distance d(y,C) from the code, find c ∈ C with d(y,c)=d(y,C). Bounded up to half the minimum distance: with the additional assumption d(y,C) ≤ (d(C)−1)/2, a codeword with the above property is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the target of all subsequent algebraic formulations: either find the nearest codeword (complete decoding) or, under the half-minimum-distance bound, find the unique nearest codeword (bounded-distance decoding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve some system S(C) in preprocessing and obtain some closed formulas CF. Evaluating these formulas at data specific to a received word r should yield a solution to the decoding problem. For example, for f ∈ CF: f(syndrome(r), x) = poly(x), whose roots give error positions (see general error-locator polynomial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic decoding requires heavy preprocessing to derive the closed formulas; once obtained, decoding for each received word is relatively simple provided the formulas are sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve a system S(C, r) that depends on the particular received word r. The solutions of this online system should directly solve the decoding problem for that r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the online decoding paradigm the hard computational effort is at decoding time (no heavy preprocessing); decoding itself is the computationally expensive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational-effort tradeoff (generic vs online)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic decoding: preprocessing is very hard while decoding is relatively simple (if the derived formulas are sparse). Online decoding: decoding is the hard part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the paradigm depending on whether one can afford heavy preprocessing to speed many decodings, or must handle each instance individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndrome computation in the cyclic-code (Cooper) setting
rubrics_metrics.description: For an [n,k] cyclic code over F_q with splitting field F and primitive n-th root a, with complete defining set S_C, a received word r=c+e yields syndromes s_{i_m}=r(a^{i_m})=e(a^{i_m}) = sum_{l=1}^t e_{j_l} (a^{j_l})^{i_m}. Defining z_l = a^{j_l} (error locations) and y_l = e_{j_l} (error values) makes the syndromes generalized power sums s_{i_m} = sum_{l=1}^t y_l z_l^{i_m}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification (syndromes as power sums in unknown locations/values) is the basis for constructing polynomial systems whose solutions reveal error positions and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRHT-syndrome ideal construction (Chen–Reed–Helleseth–Truong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variables X (syndrome variables), Z (error-location variables), Y (error-value variables) and additional auxiliary polynomials (field equations, nonzero constraints, relations linking syndromes to Z,Y) to form a set FC of polynomials in F_q[X,Z,Y]. The ideal I_C generated by FC is the CRHT-syndrome ideal; its variety V(FC) is the CRHT-syndrome variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I_C is zero-dimensional under the natural restrictions; solving (or computing a Gröbner basis of) I_C yields the error locations and values. The construction explicitly lists the polynomial constraints (syndrome equations, field equations, nonzero-value constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: General error-locator polynomial (existence and evaluation property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every cyclic code C possesses a general error-locator polynomial L_C ∈ F_q[X_1,...,X_{n-k}, Z] satisfying: (1) L_C = Z^e + a_{t-1} Z^{e-1} + ... + a_0 with a_j ∈ F_q[X_1,...,X_{n-k}] (e = error-correcting capacity); (2) given a syndrome s corresponding to an error of weight t ≤ e with error locations {k_1,...,k_t}, evaluating X_u = s_u yields that the roots of L_C(s,Z) are exactly a_{k_1},...,a_{k_t} and 0 with multiplicity e−t, i.e. L_C(s,Z)=Z^{e-t} ∏_{i=1}^t (Z − a_{k_i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general error-locator polynomial belongs to the reduced Gröbner basis of the appropriate ideal; once obtained, decoding reduces to univariate factorization of L_C(s,Z) (see sysCRHT examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the minimum distance via JC(w) systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the system J_C(w) (for binary cyclic codes with defining set S_C) consisting of polynomial equations that enforce the existence of a weight-w word supported on the defining set and field equations Z_i^n − 1 = 0 etc., together with a specified polynomial p(n,Z_i,Z_j). The number of solutions of J_C(w) equals w! times the number of codewords of weight w. For 1 ≤ w ≤ d, J_C(w) has no solutions iff w < d, and has solutions iff w = d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solving J_C(w) for successive w yields the minimum distance d; see sysCRHTMindist for examples and the referenced literature for p and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized Newton identities relating syndromes and locator coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If the error-locator polynomial σ(Z) = ∏_{l=1}^t (Z − z_l) = Z^t + σ_1 Z^{t-1} + ... + σ_t, then the syndromes s_i and the coefficients σ_j satisfy the generalized Newton identities s_i + sum_{j=1}^t σ_j s_{i-j} = 0 for all i ∈ Z_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities provide linear/nonlinear relations used to build polynomial systems (sysNewton) where syndromes are treated as variables and σ_j are unknowns; they are central to methods that recover locator coefficients from syndromes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding up to the error-correcting capacity — system constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: To decode up to capacity, introduce variables S_1,...,S_n (syndromes) and σ_1,...,σ_t (locator coefficients) and impose field and periodicity equations (S_{i+n} − S_i = 0; S_i^q − S_{qi} = 0), equalities σ_{i}^{q^m} − σ_i for 1 ≤ i ≤ t as needed, the generalized Newton identities S_i + sum_{j=1}^t σ_j S_{i-j} = 0 for all i ∈ Z_n, and the constraints S_i − s_i(r) = 0 for i ∈ S_C (known syndrome positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a finite polynomial system (see sysNewton) whose solutions correspond to admissible error patterns of weight ≤ e; references discuss the Waring-function approach as an alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitzgerald–Lax method for decoding affine-variety (affine) codes
rubrics_metrics.description: View any q-ary [n,k] linear code C as an affine variety code C(I,L) by choosing s with q^s ≥ n, distinct points P_1,...,P_n in F_q^s, construct an ideal I vanishing on these points and L a vector space spanned by evaluation functions f_i = sum_j g_{ij} ξ_j. For decoding, form the ideal I_d^C in variables corresponding to error positions and values, generated by equations ∑_{j=1}^n E_j f_i(X_j) − s_i (1 ≤ i ≤ n−k), the vanishing polynomials g_l(X_{jk}), and field equations E^{q−1} − 1 = 0. Compute the reduced Gröbner basis G of I_d^C with respect to an elimination order (X11 < ... < X1s < E1); then apply elimination theory to recover error locations and values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method generalizes the CRHT approach to affine-variety codes; the theorem asserts that elimination of the Gröbner basis yields the desired error information (see sysFL examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding method based on quadratic equations (MDS-basis approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a basis b_1,...,b_n of F_q^n and let B be the matrix with these basis rows. Define the unknown syndrome u(B,e)=B e^T and suppose b_1,...,b_n form an MDS-ordered basis (all s×s minors of leading s rows full rank). Express the known syndromes s_i(r)=∑_j a_{ij} u_j(e) where H = A B. Define U_{ij} = ∑_{l=1}^n µ_{ij}^l U_l (structure constants µ) and form the ideal J(r) generated by ∑_{l} a_{jl} U_l − s_j(r) (1 ≤ j ≤ n−k). Define I(t,U,V) by the quadratic relations ∑_{j=1}^t U_{ij} V_j − U_{i,t+1} (1 ≤ i ≤ n). Let J(t,r) be the ideal generated by J(r) and I(t,U,V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main theorem: if wt(e) ≠ 0 and wt(e) ≤ (d(C)−1)/2, and t is the smallest positive integer such that J(t,r) has a solution over the algebraic closure, then wt(e)=t and the solution is unique of multiplicity one satisfying u = u(e). The reduced Gröbner basis G of J(t,r) (w.r.t any monomial ordering) has the shape U_i − u_i(e) and V_j − v_j, enabling direct recovery of unknown syndromes and auxiliary variables (see sysQE for examples).
